title: Express configuration and CORS
idea: CORS is a browser rule: a page may read a reply from another origin (scheme, host, port) only if that server's headers allow the page's origin.
points: `express.json()` and `express.urlencoded()` fill `req.body` from JSON and form bodies.
`cors()` adds headers that tell the browser which origins may read replies.
Cookies need `credentials: true`, and browsers reject `*` as the allowed origin.

messages.label: OPTIONS (preflight)
messages.note: A JSON `POST` is not a simple request. The browser first asks permission, naming its origin.

messages.label: 204 + Allow headers
messages.note: `cors` answers 204 with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`. The browser checks them.

messages.label: POST + cookies
messages.note: If the origin is allowed, the browser sends the real request, with cookies because credentials were asked for.

messages.label: response
messages.note: Only now can the script read the body. If the origin was refused, it gets a network error instead.

pitfalls: Clients must opt in: `fetch` needs `credentials: 'include'`, or cookies are neither sent nor stored.
Browsers enforce CORS; curl and Postman ignore it. It never replaces authentication.
Set `CORS_ORIGIN`. Unset, `cors` adds no headers, so browsers block cross-origin pages.

quiz.why: The route replied before `cors` ran, so no CORS header was set. `headers.get` returns `null` for a missing header.

takeaway: The browser enforces CORS; your server only declares which origins it allows.
